star.title: Star
star.text: Stars are heated by nuclear fusion in their cores, which releases energy. Our Sun is a star. Markers from the Gaia catalog are stars, and so are SIMBAD objects that the SIMBAD object-type table groups as plain stars.

sources.label: How SIMBAD object types map to our types

brown_dwarf.title: Brown dwarf
brown_dwarf.text: Brown dwarfs form from collapsing clouds of gas, like stars do, but they are not massive enough to keep hydrogen fusion going in their cores. Brown dwarfs that drift alone in space are heated entirely from within and glow only dimly. SPHEREx is an infrared space telescope that is finding thousands of brown dwarfs. Objects that SIMBAD lists as brown dwarfs or brown dwarf candidates get this label.

sources.label: NASA: SPHEREx Telescope Sees Menagerie of Brown Dwarfs
How SIMBAD object types map to our types

variable_star.title: Variable star
variable_star.text: A star is called variable if we can measure its brightness changing over time, because of things happening inside, on the surface of, or around the star. Mira variables, for example, are giant stars whose brightness rises and falls over a cycle of roughly 80 to 1,000 days. Markers from the AAVSO VSX catalog, and SIMBAD objects listed as variable stars, use this label.

sources.label: AAVSO: Variable Stars and the Stories they Tell
AAVSO VSX: variable star type designations
How SIMBAD object types map to our types

galaxy.title: Galaxy
galaxy.text: Galaxies consist of stars, planets, and vast clouds of gas and dust, all bound together by gravity. Galaxies come in a variety of shapes, mostly spirals and ellipticals, as well as irregular ones. This label also covers active galaxies, quasars and groups of galaxies from the SIMBAD catalog.

sources.label: How SIMBAD object types map to our types

asteroid.title: Asteroid
asteroid.text: Asteroids are rocky, airless remnants left over from the early formation of our solar system about 4.6 billion years ago. Most asteroids orbit the Sun between Mars and Jupiter, in the main asteroid belt. Asteroids move during a visit, so their markers appear only on single images, never on the stacked pictures. Each marker is a position predicted by JPL's Small-Body Identification service as seen from the center of the Earth, so it can be off by up to about one pixel.

young_star.title: Young star
young_star.text: A star begins as a protostar, and at first most of its energy comes from heat released as it collapses. T Tauri stars are young stars, typically less than 10 million years old, and they vary in brightness both randomly and periodically. Young stellar objects, T Tauri stars and similar objects from SIMBAD get this label.

sources.label: NASA: Hubble observes a ghostly cloud alive with star formation
How SIMBAD object types map to our types

unknown.title: Unknown object
unknown.text: This label is used when the catalog gives no clear object type, or a type that does not fit our other labels, such as gas clouds or X-ray sources. Follow the catalog link in the panel to read what astronomers know about it.

sources.label: How SIMBAD object types map to our types

moves_as_expected.title: Moves as expected
moves_as_expected.text: SPHEREx shows the object moving, and the motion matches what the catalog predicts. The measured position follows the expected position. How this is decided: The measured motion differs from zero by more than 3 sigma, adds up to at least 0.25 pixel over the data, and agrees with the catalog motion within 3 sigma.

moves_unexpected.title: Moves unexpectedly
moves_unexpected.text: SPHEREx shows the object moving in a way the catalog does not predict. Check the measured positions and their errors before deciding what this means. How this is decided: Motion is detected as for 'moves as expected', but it is more than 3 sigma away from the catalog motion.

no_motion_detected.title: No motion detected
no_motion_detected.text: No motion larger than the measurement error was found. The object may be standing still, or moving too slowly for these pictures to show. How this is decided: The data could have detected a 1-pixel shift, but no motion was found, and brightness does not change significantly.

brightness_changes.title: Brightness changes
brightness_changes.text: The object's brightness changes between visits. Compare only images taken at nearly the same wavelength when judging brightness. How this is decided: No motion was found, but brightness differs between visits by more than 3 sigma after accounting for wavelength and for the variation of isolated stars.

saturated.title: Too bright to measure
saturated.text: The object saturates the detector in most images, so its motion can't be measured reliably. Any positions and brightness shown are less precise than for fainter objects. How this is decided: Motion can't be measured (a 1-pixel shift would not be detectable) and the object is saturated in more than half of its images.

too_faint.title: Too faint to measure
too_faint.text: The object is too faint to measure in these images. No position or brightness is shown for it. How this is decided: Motion can't be measured and the object is mostly not saturated, so it is too faint.

epsilon_indi_b.title: Epsilon Indi B
epsilon_indi_b.text: Epsilon Indi B is a pair of brown dwarfs, called Ba and Bb. It travels through space together with the star Epsilon Indi. It is one of the fastest-moving objects outside our solar system: the Gaia catalog measures its motion at about 4.7 arcseconds per year, toward the east and south. On the pictures, look for its marker drifting left and down by about three quarters of a pixel each year.

barnards_star.title: Barnard's Star
barnards_star.text: Barnard's Star is a red dwarf about 6 light-years away, and it is the closest single star to the Sun. It has the largest apparent motion of any known star: the Gaia catalog measures about 10.4 arcseconds per year, mostly toward the north. On the pictures, look for its marker climbing upward, slightly to the right, by about 1.7 pixels each year. It is a bright star, so some images may be saturated; check the verdict.

r_draconis.title: R Draconis
r_draconis.text: R Draconis is a Mira-type variable star: a giant star whose brightness rises and falls over a cycle of about 246 days. Bright stars can saturate the detector pixels, so R Draconis may show up as saturated when it is near its brightest. Its own motion across the sky is tiny: the Gaia catalog measures only about 0.02 arcseconds per year, toward the west and a little north. So look for its brightness changing between visits, not for its marker moving.

sources.label: AAVSO VSX: variable star type designations

rw_aurigae.title: RW Aurigae
rw_aurigae.text: RW Aurigae is a young binary star, two stars called A and B that orbit close together. In the Gaia catalog the two stars are only about 1.5 arcseconds apart, much less than one 6.15-arcsecond pixel, so they blend into a single dot. RW Aur A faded dramatically twice, in 2010-11 and again from 2014 to 2016, and astronomers explain this as dust passing in front of the star. Its own motion across the sky is tiny, about 0.03 arcseconds per year, so look for brightness changes between visits instead.

wise_0855.title: WISE 0855
wise_0855.text: WISE 0855 is an extremely cold brown dwarf: a 2014 study estimated its temperature at only 225 to 260 kelvin, about -48 to -13 degrees Celsius, the coldest known for a brown dwarf at that time. It is only about 7 light-years from the Sun, and in 2014 it had the third-highest motion of any known star or brown dwarf, about 8.1 arcseconds per year. The catalog motion shown here is from Kirkpatrick et al. (2021): -8124 milliarcseconds per year in right ascension (toward the west) and +673 in declination (slightly north). On the pictures, west is to the right, so look for its marker drifting right.

how_it_works.title: See the sky move, and know how far to trust it
how_it_works.text: SPHEREx is a NASA telescope that maps the whole sky in 102 colors about every six months. This tool lines up every SPHEREx image of one patch of sky, shows you what changed between visits, and measures it. Every measurement is checked against stars whose answer is already known, so you can see how accurate it is.

cards.title: Watch
cards.text: Flip or blink between visits about six months apart. Nearby stars and brown dwarfs creep across the frame, and variable stars brighten and fade.

cards.title: Measure
cards.text: We measure the target's position in every single image (461 for Epsilon Indi B) and fit its motion with error bars. Brightness is compared between visits after accounting for the color each image was taken in.

cards.title: Check
cards.text: Every Gaia star in the field is measured the same way and compared with where Gaia predicts it. Each field gets two verdicts, one for the target and one for how accurate its stars are.

cards.title: Search anywhere
cards.text: Type any object name or coordinates. The server pulls the SPHEREx images from the archive and builds the field in a few minutes.

limits.title: What this tool can't tell you
limits.text: Small motions. Each pixel is 6.15 arcseconds wide, and SPHEREx has watched each target for only one to one and a half years so far. We call something moving only when its shift adds up to at least 0.25 pixel (1.5 arcseconds) over the data and is more than 3 sigma from zero. Slower objects can be real movers that this tool can't see yet. Very bright stars. Bright stars fill up the detector. SPHEREx still estimates their brightness from readouts taken before that happens, so we keep measuring them, with larger errors (hollow points in the charts). Barnard's Star is saturated in 93% of its images and its motion is still measured. When more than half of a target's images are saturated and its motion can't be pinned down, as for R Draconis, we say so instead of giving a motion verdict. Faint objects. When a target is too faint to measure in single images, we fit all of a visit's images at once. This works for WISE 0855, but its motion carries an error of about 14% (8350 plus or minus 1174 milliarcseconds per year in right ascension). Crowded fields. Most tested field stars (59 of 73) have another Gaia star within 2 pixels. Their light blends, which shifts where each star appears to sit by a constant amount. A constant shift can't create motion, so the motion test removes it. An unresolved pair whose stars change brightness can also shift its light center (RW Aurigae: 0.07 pixel), which is why a shift must reach 0.25 pixel before we call it motion. Error bars. Tested on field stars, our error bars are slightly too small. The real scatter is about 1.4 times the error bar over all fields and 1.7 times in the crowded Barnard's Star field. The line between a field that is mostly accurate and one with some stars off (20% of stars not matching) is our judgment call, so the counts are always shown next to the label. Colors and brightness. Each single image is taken at a different wavelength, so brightness changes between single images are expected. We compare brightness only between visits, after accounting for wavelength. Field-star brightness isn't checked against any catalog yet. Difference images. A red and blue pair in a difference image is not proof of motion. Stars aren't equally bright at every wavelength, so a star that hasn't moved can leave a pair when two visits used different detectors. Check the measured positions instead. Long wavelengths. Images at 4 to 5 micrometers are noisier, so color images show faint red speckle that is not a real source. Catalog markers. Asteroid markers are predictions, and catalog markers can be out of date or wrong. Sources that appear in no catalog aren't flagged yet. New positions. Any position can be searched, but it is built from the SPHEREx archive on request. That takes several minutes and needs the archive to be online. A position with no catalog motion gets no motion comparison, only the field check.

methodology.title: How we measure
methodology.text: Images. For each field we take every SPHEREx image that covers it, from every public release, and cut out the field. Each image records one wavelength at each point on the detector, so we record the exact wavelength at the target in every image. Cleaning. We subtract the model of zodiacal light (sunlight scattered by interplanetary dust) supplied with each image, then any remaining smooth background, and blank the pixels the quality flags mark as unusable. Saturated pixels are kept: SPHEREx estimates their brightness from readouts taken before the detector filled up, so they are usable but less precise. Visits and pictures. Images more than 30 days apart belong to different visits. All images are placed on one grid with north up, and each visit's images are averaged into one picture, rejecting values far from the rest (cosmic rays, asteroids). These pictures are for looking at; we don't measure on them. Color pictures combine 0.75-1.6 micrometers (blue), 1.6-3.8 micrometers (green) and 3.8-5.0 micrometers (red). Positions. We measure each object in every single image, in that image's own pixels, because resampling blurs positions. A brighter catalog star close by is fitted at the same time at its known position, so it can't pull the measurement. The expected position comes from Gaia DR3, moved to the image's date using the star's motion and parallax (for WISE 0855, which Gaia can't see, from Kirkpatrick et al. 2021). Error bars. Each field contains isolated stars with very precise Gaia positions. Their scatter around those positions is added to every error bar, so the errors include everything that affects real measurements, not only the fit. Images from the same visit also share a small error (about 0.02 pixel) that averaging can't remove, and we include it. Motion. We fit a straight line through the measured positions over time, after removing the yearly parallax wobble the catalog predicts. Brightness. Because each image is at a different wavelength, we compare brightness between visits only after accounting for wavelength, and against how much the isolated stars' brightness changes from visit to visit. Very faint objects. When a target is too faint to measure in single images (WISE 0855), we fit SPHEREx's own model of a star's image to all of a visit's images at once. The 0.25 pixel minimum for motion exists because an unresolved pair's light center shifts when one star changes brightness (RW Aurigae: 0.07 pixel), which isn't motion.
